name: picoquic
workload: quicperf loopback harness: QUIC client-to-server bulk Upload scenario, CUBIC congestion control, syscall UDP backend, 2 client threads, both rows publishable status.
claimed_speedup: 15.823 Gbps p50 (picoquic) vs 14.794 Gbps p50 (quiche) on the Upload scenario, ~7% faster (derived from page data); also 297 vs 277 connections/second p50 on the Connect scenario, ~7% faster (derived from page data)
compiler_and_flags: quicperf CMake Release build: -O3, native CPU flags, LTO by default; exact compiler/version not published
tradeoffs: picoquic is a minimal, largely single-threaded reference/research QUIC stack. It only leads quiche on 2 of 16 quicperf scenarios (Upload throughput, Connect rate); quiche wins the other 14, often by a wide margin (e.g. request/response 64,574 vs 59,098 qps, stream churn 74,756 vs 48,480 streams/s), so this is workload-specific, not general superiority.
caveats: quicperf (victorstewart/quicperf) is an independent third-party multi-stack QUIC benchmark harness, not picoquic's or quiche's own benchmark. CPU model is not published in the harness's README, methodology.md, or results doc, so the entry is capped at tier B despite public benchmark code and stated build flags. Both compared rows carry the harness's own 'publishable' (passed audit gates) status.
found_via: GitHub: victorstewart/quicperf docs/latest-results.md, Upload and Connect scenario tables (orchestrator-flagged quicperf harness)

name: quic-zig
workload: quicperf loopback harness: QUIC Connect scenario (full handshake + first stream creation), CUBIC congestion control, syscall UDP backend, 8 client threads, both rows publishable status.
claimed_speedup: 286 connections/second p50 (quic-zig) vs 277 connections/second p50 (quiche), ~3% faster (derived from page data)
compiler_and_flags: Zig packet engine built with ReleaseFast; C++ harness UDP I/O built -O3/native/LTO; exact zig compiler version not published
tradeoffs: quic-zig is a young Zig QUIC packet engine (the C++ harness owns UDP I/O); it loses to quiche by a wide margin on nearly every other quicperf scenario (download 10.463 vs 11.258 Gbps, upload 10.642 vs 14.794 Gbps, request/response 3,716 vs 64,574 qps), so this is a narrow, workload-specific win, not general superiority.
caveats: Margin is small (~3%) and only 1 of 16 quicperf scenarios favors quic-zig over quiche. CPU model is not published in the harness docs, so tier is capped at B. Treat as a marginal result pending independent reproduction.
found_via: GitHub: victorstewart/quicperf docs/latest-results.md, Connect scenario table (orchestrator-flagged quicperf harness)

name: Unbound
workload: Cache-hit DNS query throughput: www.nlnetlabs.nl served from cache, with and without the DO (DNSSEC OK) bit set.
claimed_speedup: 31,218.3 qps (Unbound) vs 8,987.99 qps (BIND) with no DO bit; 28,735.6 qps (Unbound) vs 8,269.31 qps (BIND) with DO bit set -- roughly 3.4x faster cache-hit throughput than BIND (also noted as roughly on par with NSD: 36,048.4 vs 35,182.8 qps on an NXDOMAIN/NSEC3 workload)
tradeoffs: Unbound is a validating recursive/caching resolver, not an authoritative server like BIND or NSD, so the roles only overlap for the cache-hit/recursive-resolution path measured here.
caveats: This is a first-party developer changelog entry dated 22 February 2008, comparing Unbound to a BIND version of that era; no CPU model, compiler, or exact BIND version is stated, and the result is 18 years old so it may not reflect current BIND/Unbound performance.
found_via: GitHub code search: 'faster than BIND' -> NLnetLabs/unbound doc/Changelog

name: Hickory DNS (formerly Trust-DNS)
workload: Single UDP DNS A-record query for www.example.com against a local authoritative server, round-trip time measured with identical zone config and test client for both servers.
claimed_speedup: 68,173 ns/iter (+/- 11,699) for Trust-DNS vs 69,576 ns/iter (+/- 3,620) for BIND9 -- reached rough parity, ~2% faster median (derived from page data); down from an initial ~400us vs ~100us gap before optimization
compiler_and_flags: Rust nightly, release build (cargo bench); exact rustc version not stated
hardware: author's laptop (macOS), no CPU model given
tradeoffs: The final result is closer to parity than a clear win (~2%); the post itself frames the goal as 'making trust-dns fast [enough]' rather than definitively faster. BIND has far more production features (dynamic reconfiguration, extensive DNSSEC signing, etc.) not exercised in this microbenchmark.
caveats: Author explicitly calls the approach non-scientific; hardware is only described as 'an older laptop', no CPU model or BIND version pinned. Benchmark code is public in a linked PR (#317) but methodology is informal, capping the tier at C.
found_via: GitHub code search: 'faster than BIND9' -> rust-lang/this-week-in-rust linking bluejekyll's Trust-DNS blog post

name: Nail (NailDNS demo server)
workload: Authoritative-DNS-server load test: random zone file (50,000 domains) and random query sequence with 10% NXDOMAIN, run for one minute against a Nail-generated DNS server and against BIND 9.5.5 on the same local machine.
claimed_speedup: median throughput ~139,215 qps (NailDNS) vs ~47,234 qps (BIND 9.5.5), approximately 3x faster; median per-query latency 0.139 ms vs 0.416 ms (derived from page data, box-plot figure)
tradeoffs: NailDNS is a 295-line research demo built to showcase the Nail parser-combinator toolkit (grammar-driven parsing/generation with dependent fields and stream transforms); it implements only zone parsing, query answering, and label compression, none of BIND's dynamic reconfiguration, TSIG, notify, or DNSSEC-signing machinery. Not a drop-in BIND replacement.
caveats: Peer-reviewed OSDI'14 paper (USENIX) with raw box-plot data embedded in the LaTeX source, but no CPU model or compiler/flags are stated anywhere in the paper or repo, capping the tier at B. Benchmark is against BIND 9.5.5, a release from 2009; project has been unmaintained since 2020. Set usability to 'reference' since the demo server is a minimal example, not intended as a production DNS library.
found_via: GitHub code search: 'times faster than BIND' -> jbangert/nail paper/login/eval.tex and paper/osdi14/performance.tex

name: Bundy-DNS (l1cache experimental branch)
workload: Experimental fully-rendered response cache ('jinmei-l1cache' branch): hash-table keyed by query name+type storing pre-rendered wire-format responses, benchmarked as an authoritative-server cache-hit path.
claimed_speedup: 'more than 4 times faster than BIND 9' on the cache-hit path (no exact qps numbers given)
tradeoffs: The design doc itself cautions 'as usual, the comparison is not entirely fair'; the l1cache approach was an experimental idea documented on a named developer branch, not confirmed as merged into Bundy's mainline default response path. Bundy is a community continuation of the discontinued ISC BIND10 project.
caveats: First-party design-document claim with a round number ('4 times') but no methodology, workload size, hardware, or exact qps figures. The bundy-dns/bundy repo shows a recent push date but overall project activity is very low (community-maintained fork of the abandoned BIND10 project); treat the 'active' recency as a minor-maintenance signal, not sustained development.
found_via: GitHub code search: 'faster than BIND' -> bundy-dns/bundy doc/design/resolver/03-cache-algorithm
